questions.q: Which plane divides the body into front (anterior) and back (posterior) portions?
questions.e: The coronal (frontal) plane splits front from back.

questions.q: Which plane is also called the horizontal plane?
questions.e: Transverse = horizontal plane; it divides top from bottom.

questions.q: Which plane divides the body into EQUAL left and right halves?
questions.e: The midsagittal (median) plane runs directly through the center.

questions.q: The transverse plane divides the body into:
questions.e: Transverse (horizontal) = superior vs. inferior.

questions.q: The coronal plane is also known as the:
questions.e: Coronal a.k.a. frontal.

questions.q: A plane that divides the body into UNEQUAL left and right pieces is a:
questions.e: Sagittal = left/right pieces; midsagittal is the special case that makes equal halves.

questions.q: The midsagittal plane is a special type of which plane?
questions.e: Midsagittal (median) = a sagittal plane through the exact center.

questions.q: Which plane divides the body at various angles?
questions.e: Oblique (angular) plane cuts at various angles.

questions.q: Anatomy is the study of the body's:
questions.e: Anatomy = STRUCTURE (names of parts and regions).

questions.q: Physiology is the study of:
questions.e: Physiology = how the body FUNCTIONS and how parts work together.

questions.q: Describing HOW the kidneys filter waste from blood is an example of:
questions.e: How something works = function = physiology.

questions.q: Learning the names of the bones of the skull is an example of:
questions.e: Names of parts = structure = anatomy.

questions.q: Explaining how the heart pumps blood through the body is:
questions.e: Pumping is a function, so it's physiology.

questions.q: Identifying the four chambers of the heart is:
questions.e: Identifying parts = structure = anatomy.

questions.q: Why are anatomy and physiology studied together?
w: Function determines the names of parts
questions.e: The lecture's spoon/fork/knife example: a part's structure determines what it can do.

questions.q: Which statement is correct?
w: Both mean the study of function
Both mean the study of structure
questions.e: Anatomy = STRUCTURE; physiology = FUNCTION.

questions.q: Losing electrons in a chemical reaction is called:
questions.e: LEO: Lose Electrons = Oxidation.

questions.q: Gaining electrons in a chemical reaction is called:
questions.e: GER: Gain Electrons = Reduction.

questions.q: When sodium (Na) loses an electron and becomes Na⁺, sodium has been:
questions.e: Na loses an electron, so it is oxidized (LEO).

questions.q: When chlorine (Cl) gains an electron and becomes Cl⁻, chlorine has been:
questions.e: Cl gains an electron, so it is reduced (GER).

questions.q: In the memory aid 'LEO the lion goes GER', what does LEO stand for?
questions.e: LEO = Lose Electrons = Oxidation; GER = Gain Electrons = Reduction.

questions.q: Which statement about oxidation and reduction is TRUE?
w: They never occur in the same reaction
questions.e: An oxidation must be coupled with a reduction, and vice versa.

questions.q: In GER, the 'R' stands for:
questions.e: Gain Electrons = Reduction.

questions.q: An atom that becomes more NEGATIVE by picking up an electron has undergone:
questions.e: Gaining an electron (more negative charge) = reduction.

questions.q: Atomic number is equal to the number of:
questions.e: Atomic number = # of protons.

questions.q: Atomic mass is equal to the number of:
questions.e: Atomic mass = protons + neutrons.

questions.q: How do you calculate the number of neutrons in an atom?
questions.e: # neutrons = atomic mass − atomic number.

questions.q: An element has an atomic number of 20. How many electrons are in a neutral atom of it?
questions.e: Neutral atoms have equal protons and electrons, so 20.

questions.q: An atom has 11 protons. How many electrons does a neutral atom of it have?
questions.e: # electrons = # protons in a neutral atom.

questions.q: Which type of bond forms when a metal gives electrons to a nonmetal?
questions.e: Ionic bonds: electrons given by a metal and received by a nonmetal.

questions.q: Which type of bond is described as STRONG?
questions.e: Covalent bonds are STRONG bonds where nonmetals share electrons.

questions.q: Which relatively WEAK bond forms between water molecules and between DNA bases?
questions.e: Hydrogen bonds are relatively weak attractions between H atoms of different molecules.

questions.q: A bond formed between a cation (+) and an anion (−) is a(n):
questions.e: Ionic bonds form between oppositely charged ions.

questions.q: Which type of bond falls apart (dissociates) easily in water?
questions.e: Ionic bonds dissociate easily in water (e.g., NaCl).

questions.q: NaCl (table salt) is held together by which type of bond?
questions.e: NaCl is the lecture's example of an ionic bond.

questions.q: A covalent bond in which electrons are shared EQUALLY (e.g., CO₂) is:
questions.e: Nonpolar covalent = equal sharing; atoms close to the same size.

questions.q: Hydrogen bonds form between:
questions.e: Hydrogen bonds: adjacent hydrogen atoms of DIFFERENT molecules.

questions.q: Which term means 'toward the head'?
questions.e: Superior, cranial and cephalic all mean toward the head.

questions.q: 'Caudal' means:
questions.e: Caudal (caudad) = toward the tail, same as inferior.

questions.q: Which pair of terms BOTH mean 'toward the head'?
questions.e: Head: superior/cranial/cephalic. Tail: inferior/caudal/caudad.

questions.q: 'Superior' is also called:
questions.e: Superior (cranial/cephalic) = toward the head.

questions.q: 'Inferior' is also called:
questions.e: Inferior (caudal/caudad) = toward the tail/feet.

questions.q: The term 'cranial' comes from cranium, which means:
questions.e: Cranium = skull → 'cranial'.

questions.q: Which term means the OPPOSITE of caudal?
questions.e: Caudal = toward tail; cranial = toward head.

questions.q: Which pair of terms BOTH mean 'toward the tail'?
questions.e: Inferior, caudal and caudad all mean toward the tail/feet.

questions.q: The smallest unit of matter is the:
questions.e: Atoms are the smallest unit of matter.

questions.q: The smallest unit of life is the:
questions.e: Cells are the smallest unit of life.

questions.q: Which pairing is correct?
questions.e: Atom = smallest unit of matter; cell = smallest unit of life.

questions.q: The study of cells, the smallest unit of life, is called:
questions.e: Cytology = study of cells. Histology = study of tissues.

questions.q: Atoms are made of which three subatomic particles?
questions.e: Atoms (smallest unit of matter) are made of protons, neutrons and electrons.

questions.q: Which is the correct order from smallest to largest?
questions.e: Levels of organization build from atoms up to the organism.

questions.q: The human body is made of roughly how many cells?
questions.e: The body is made of ~35 trillion cells, the smallest units of life.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT alive on its own, but is the smallest unit of matter?
questions.e: Atoms are matter, not life. The cell is the smallest living unit.

questions.q: Homeostasis is best defined as:
w: The breakdown of food into nutrients
The movement of water across a membrane
questions.e: Homeostasis = the process of maintaining a stable internal environment.

questions.q: Homeostasis is also known as:
questions.e: a.k.a. dynamic equilibrium or state of balance.

questions.q: In a homeostatic feedback loop, which part SENSES the change?
questions.e: Stimulus → receptor (senses) → control center → effector.

questions.q: In a feedback loop, which part interprets the signal and decides how to respond?
questions.e: The control center interprets the signal and sends instructions.

questions.q: In a feedback loop, which part carries out the response (a cell, tissue or organ)?
questions.e: The effector brings about the response; it is always a cell, tissue or organ.

questions.q: In a feedback loop, a 'stimulus' is:
questions.e: Stimulus = deviation from normal.

questions.q: Which organ systems help maintain homeostasis?
questions.e: Virtually every organ system plays a role.

questions.q: What is the correct order of a feedback loop?
questions.e: Stimulus is sensed by a receptor, interpreted by the control center, and carried out by an effector.

questions.q: An acid is a substance that:
questions.e: Acids are H⁺ donors.

questions.q: A base is a substance that:
questions.e: Bases donate OH⁻ and can be defined as H⁺ acceptors.

questions.q: In the reaction HCl → H⁺ + Cl⁻, HCl is acting as:
questions.e: HCl releases H⁺, so it's an acid.

questions.q: In the reaction NaOH → Na⁺ + OH⁻, NaOH is acting as:
questions.e: NaOH releases OH⁻, so it's a base.

questions.q: Which characteristics describe a BASE?
w: Sour taste, burns metal, pH below 7
questions.e: Bases: bitter, slippery, high pH.

questions.q: Which characteristics describe an ACID?
questions.a: Sour taste, burns through metal, pH below 7
questions.e: Acids: sour, burn through metal, low pH.

questions.q: Which substance ACCEPTS hydrogen ions?
questions.e: Bases can be defined as hydrogen ion acceptors.

questions.q: Compounds that resist dramatic changes in pH by adding or removing H⁺ are called:
questions.e: Buffers act as acids when pH is high and as bases when pH is low.

questions.q: What is the MAJOR component of the cell membrane?
questions.e: Phospholipids (bilayer) are the major component.

questions.q: Which TWO types of lipids are found in the cell membrane?
questions.e: Membrane lipids: phospholipids and cholesterol (a steroid).

questions.q: Which is NOT a component of the cell membrane?
questions.e: Membrane = phospholipids, proteins, sugars, cholesterol. Glycogen is stored in liver and muscle.

questions.q: The phospholipid head is ______ and the tail is ______.
questions.e: Head loves water (hydrophilic); tail fears water (hydrophobic).

questions.q: What role does cholesterol play in the cell membrane?
questions.a: Holds phospholipids together; gives flexible rigidity
questions.e: Cholesterol sits between phospholipids and gives 'flexible' rigidity.

questions.q: The 'fluid mosaic model' means membrane components:
questions.a: Are free to move within the membrane
questions.e: Components are not locked in place; they move within the membrane.

questions.q: Which membrane component is used for blood typing?
questions.e: Membrane sugars: cell recognition, receptors, blood typing.

questions.q: Which membrane proteins span the entire membrane and form channels?
questions.e: Integral proteins touch both inside and outside; only they form channels.

questions.q: What is the charge of a neutron?
questions.e: Neutrons have no charge.

questions.q: Which subatomic particle carries a NEGATIVE charge?
questions.e: Electrons are negative.

questions.q: Which subatomic particle carries a POSITIVE charge?
questions.e: Protons are positive.

questions.q: Which correctly matches particle and charge?
questions.e: Proton +, neutron 0, electron −.

questions.q: Which particles are found in the nucleus?
questions.e: Nucleus = protons + neutrons; electrons are in the electron cloud.

questions.q: Where are electrons found?
questions.a: In the electron cloud (shells/orbits) around the nucleus
questions.e: Electrons circle the nucleus in shells, orbits or rings.

questions.q: An atom that LOSES an electron becomes a:
questions.e: Losing electrons leaves more protons, so the atom is positive (cation).

questions.q: An atom that GAINS an electron becomes a(n):
questions.e: Gaining electrons makes it negative (anion).

questions.q: Energy of motion is called:
questions.e: Kinetic = energy of motion.

questions.q: Stored energy is called:
questions.e: Potential = stored energy.

questions.q: Heat, light and the movement of large objects are examples of:
questions.e: All are energy of motion.

questions.q: The energy held in chemical bonds is:
questions.e: Chemical bonds store energy, so it's potential.

questions.q: A charged battery sitting on a shelf contains:
questions.e: A battery is the lecture's example of stored (potential) energy.

questions.q: Energy is defined as:
questions.e: Energy is the ability to do work.

questions.q: A muscle actively contracting and moving the arm shows:
questions.e: Movement = energy of motion = kinetic.

questions.q: Which pairing is correct?
questions.e: Kinetic is motion; potential is stored.

questions.q: H₂ (two hydrogen atoms bonded together) is a:
questions.e: A molecule is one type of element only.

questions.q: A compound is made of:
questions.e: Compound = 2+ different elements.

questions.q: Methane (CH₄), made of carbon and hydrogen, is a:
questions.e: Two different elements make it a compound.

questions.q: O₂ (two oxygen atoms) is best classified as a:
questions.e: Only one type of element (oxygen), so it's a molecule.

questions.q: Water (H₂O) contains hydrogen and oxygen. It is a:
questions.e: Two different elements, so it's a compound.

questions.q: Which is the key difference between a molecule and a compound (as taught in lecture)?
questions.a: Molecule = one type of element; compound = two or more different elements
questions.e: Molecule = same element; compound = multiple elements.

questions.q: Glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆) is a:
questions.e: Three different elements (C, H, O), so it's a compound.

questions.q: N₂ (two nitrogen atoms) is a:
questions.e: One type of element only, so it's a molecule.

questions.q: Which is an example of POSITIVE feedback?
questions.e: Positive feedback examples: childbirth (oxytocin) and blood clotting.

questions.q: In NEGATIVE feedback, the response:
questions.a: Moves in the opposite direction of the change
w: Moves in the same direction as the change
questions.e: Negative feedback counteracts the stimulus.

questions.q: Shivering to warm up when you are cold is an example of:
questions.e: The response opposes the change, so it's negative feedback.

questions.q: Most feedback mechanisms in the body are:
questions.e: Most feedback is negative.

questions.q: In POSITIVE feedback, the response:
questions.e: Positive feedback amplifies and drives farther from normal.

questions.q: Blood clotting is an example of:
questions.e: Blood clotting is a positive feedback example.

questions.q: Sweating when body temperature rises is an example of:
questions.e: Sweating cools the body, opposing the rise.

questions.q: Which hormone drives the positive feedback loop of childbirth?
questions.e: The pituitary releases oxytocin, amplifying contractions.

questions.q: The liquid portion of the cytoplasm is the:
questions.e: Cytoplasm includes cytosol (liquid), organelles, inclusions.

questions.q: Which is NOT part of the cytoplasm?
questions.e: The nucleus is its own component.

questions.q: The three main components of a cell are:
questions.e: Membrane ('skin'), cytoplasm ('guts'), nucleus ('brain').

questions.q: The cytoplasm is described as the cell's:
questions.e: Cytoplasm = the 'guts' of the cell.

questions.q: The nucleus is described as the cell's:
questions.e: Nucleus = 'brain' / command center.

questions.q: Tiny 'organs' inside the cell are called:
questions.e: Organelles = tiny organs within the cytoplasm.

questions.q: Things inside the cytoplasm that do NOT dissolve in water, like fat and pigments, are:
questions.e: Inclusions = undissolved things like fat and pigment.

questions.q: The cytoplasm includes which three things?
questions.e: Cytoplasm = cytosol + organelles + inclusions.

questions.q: Glucose is classified as a:
questions.e: Glucose, fructose, galactose = monosaccharides.

questions.q: Sucrose (glucose + fructose) is a:
questions.e: Disaccharides: sucrose, lactose, maltose.

questions.q: Glycogen, the storage form of glucose in animals, is a:
questions.e: Polysaccharides: starch (plants), glycogen (animals).

questions.q: Lactose is made of:
questions.e: Lactose = glucose + galactose.

questions.q: Maltose is made of:
questions.e: Maltose = glucose + glucose.

questions.q: Starch, the storage form of carbohydrate in plants, is a:
questions.e: Starch = plant polysaccharide.

questions.q: A disaccharide is made of how many monosaccharides?
questions.e: Di = 2.

questions.q: Which chemical reaction joins monosaccharides into a disaccharide?
questions.e: Monosaccharides are combined by dehydration synthesis.

questions.q: Where is glycogen stored in the body?
questions.e: Glycogen is stored in skeletal muscle and liver.

questions.q: Which is a monosaccharide?
questions.e: Fructose is a simple sugar; the others are di- or polysaccharides.

questions.q: In which type of bond are electrons SHARED?
questions.e: Covalent bonds: nonmetals share electrons.

questions.q: In which type of bond does one atom take ('steal') electrons from another?
questions.e: Ionic: electrons are given by one atom and received by another.

questions.q: In water, oxygen and hydrogen share electrons UNEQUALLY. This is a:
questions.e: Polar covalent = unequal sharing (e.g., water).

questions.q: Sharing electrons equally between atoms of about the same size is a:
questions.e: Nonpolar covalent = equal sharing (e.g., CO₂).

questions.q: Covalent bonds form between:
w: A metal and a nonmetal transferring electrons
questions.e: Covalent = two or more nonmetals sharing.

questions.q: Polar covalent bonds share electrons unequally because:
questions.a: The atoms are very different in size
w: The atoms are the same size
questions.e: Large difference in atom size → unequal sharing.

questions.q: When Na gives its electron to Cl to form NaCl, the bond formed is:
questions.e: Electron transferred (not shared), so it's ionic.

questions.q: A chemical bond is an attraction between atoms created by:
questions.e: Bonds form by sharing, losing or gaining electrons.

questions.q: AB + CD → AC + BD is an example of:
questions.e: Partners are swapped, so it's an exchange reaction.

questions.q: A + B + energy ⇄ AB is an example of a:
questions.e: The double arrow means either direction.

questions.q: A + B → AB is an example of:
questions.e: Putting pieces together = synthesis.

questions.q: A + BC → AC + B is an example of:
questions.e: One element replaces another in a compound.

questions.q: AB → A + B + energy is an example of:
questions.e: Breaking down, releasing energy = decomposition (catabolic).

questions.q: A double displacement reaction is actually a combination of which two reactions?
questions.e: AB + CD breaks apart (catabolic) and then recombines (anabolic).

questions.q: Metal on a car slowly rusting is the lecture's example of a:
questions.e: Most reactions in nature are reversible, even if it takes years.

questions.q: Which statement about reversible reactions is TRUE?
questions.a: Most reactions in nature are reversible
questions.e: Most natural reactions are reversible.

questions.q: Which substance is known as the 'universal solvent'?
questions.e: Water is the universal solvent.

questions.q: Water makes up about how much of your body weight?
questions.e: ~2/3 of body weight.

questions.q: A solvent is a substance that:
questions.e: Solvent: dissolves things.

questions.q: Water is held together by which type of bond?
questions.e: Water is an inorganic compound with polar covalent bonds.

questions.q: Water is classified as a(n):
questions.e: Water contains no carbon, so it is inorganic.

questions.q: Which is NOT a function of water in the body?
questions.e: Water: solvent, lubrication/cushioning, temperature regulation, transport. DNA stores genetic info.

questions.q: Water helps regulate body temperature through:
questions.a: Sweat and its high heat capacity
questions.e: Temperature regulator: sweat and high heat capacity.

questions.q: Why is water called the 'universal solvent'?
questions.a: It dissolves more substances than any other liquid
w: It is found everywhere in the universe
questions.e: Water's polarity lets it dissolve a huge range of substances.

questions.q: Which term does NOT refer to the head?
questions.e: Caudal = toward the tail.

questions.q: Which term means 'toward the tail'?
questions.e: Caudad/caudal/inferior = tail.

questions.q: 'Cephalic' refers to the:
questions.e: Cephalon = head.

questions.q: Which term does NOT refer to the tail/feet?
questions.e: Cranial = toward the head.

questions.q: Which group contains ONLY 'head' words?
questions.e: Head: superior, cranial, cephalic.

questions.q: Which group contains ONLY 'tail' words?
questions.e: Tail: inferior, caudal, caudad.

questions.q: 'Cephalon' is the Latin/Greek word for:
questions.e: Cephalon (head) → 'cephalic'. Cranium = skull.

questions.q: The feet are ______ to the head.
questions.e: Toward the tail/feet = inferior/caudal.

questions.q: The pH scale ranges from:
questions.e: pH range is 0–14.

questions.q: The normal pH of human blood is:
questions.e: Blood pH = 7.35–7.45 (slightly basic).

questions.q: As H⁺ concentration INCREASES, a solution becomes more:
questions.e: More H⁺ = more acidic = lower pH.

questions.q: As OH⁻ concentration INCREASES, a solution becomes more:
questions.e: More OH⁻ = more basic = higher pH.

questions.q: Human blood (pH 7.35–7.45) is:
questions.e: Just above 7 = slightly basic.

questions.q: Osmosis is the movement of:
w: Gases from high to low concentration
Particles through holes driven by blood pressure
questions.e: Osmosis = 'the diffusion of water'.

questions.q: Simple diffusion is the movement of molecules:
questions.a: From high to low concentration without energy
w: From low to high concentration using ATP
questions.e: Diffusion: high → low, down a concentration gradient, no energy.

questions.q: What is the key difference between diffusion and osmosis?
questions.a: Osmosis moves only water; diffusion moves other molecules
w: Diffusion requires ATP; osmosis does not
Diffusion moves low to high; osmosis high to low
Osmosis is active; diffusion is passive
questions.e: Both are passive and high → low; osmosis is water only.

questions.q: Diffusion and osmosis are both examples of:
questions.e: Both are passive.

questions.q: A cell placed in a HYPOTONIC solution will:
questions.e: Water rushes in, so the cell swells.

questions.q: A cell placed in a HYPERTONIC solution will:
questions.e: Water moves out, so the cell shrinks.

questions.q: In an ISOTONIC solution, a cell will:
questions.e: Same concentration inside and out, so water moves evenly.

questions.q: Simple diffusion is driven by:
questions.e: Diffusion is driven by a concentration gradient.

questions.q: The sagittal plane divides the body into:
questions.e: Sagittal = left/right.

questions.q: The frontal plane is another name for the:
questions.e: Coronal a.k.a. frontal.

questions.q: Which plane is also called the angular plane?
questions.e: Oblique = angular.

questions.q: A cut that separates the face from the back of the head is along the:
questions.e: Front vs. back = coronal (frontal).

questions.q: A cut that separates the right eye from the left eye is along a:
questions.e: Left vs. right = sagittal.

questions.q: A cut at the waist separating the upper body from the lower body is along the:
questions.e: Top vs. bottom = transverse (horizontal).

questions.q: The median plane is another name for the:
questions.e: Midsagittal (median).

questions.q: Which pairing is correct?
questions.e: Coronal splits front/back; sagittal splits left/right.

questions.q: 'Medial' means:
w: Close to the point of attachment
questions.e: Medial = toward the midline.

questions.q: The wrist is ______ to the elbow.
questions.e: Distal = farther from the point of attachment.

questions.q: The ears are ______ to the nose.
questions.e: Lateral = away from the midline.

questions.q: The elbow is ______ to the wrist.
questions.e: Proximal = closer to the point of attachment.

questions.q: 'Superficial' means:
questions.e: Superficial (external) = toward the surface.

questions.q: The skin is ______ to the muscles.
questions.e: The skin is closer to the surface.

questions.q: 'Anterior' is also called:
questions.e: Anterior (ventral) = toward the front.

questions.q: 'Posterior' is also called:
questions.e: Posterior (dorsal) = toward the back.

questions.q: The nose is ______ to the eyes.
questions.e: The nose is closer to the midline.

questions.q: The term for 'between superficial and deep' is:
questions.e: Intermediate = between superficial and deep.

questions.q: Which statement about synthesis reactions is TRUE?
questions.a: They build larger molecules and require energy
questions.e: Synthesis (anabolic) = construction; requires energy.

questions.q: Dehydration synthesis creates a bond by:
questions.e: Dehydration = removal of water.

questions.q: Synthesis reactions are also called:
questions.e: Synthesis = anabolic; decomposition = catabolic.

questions.q: Which equation represents a synthesis reaction?
questions.e: Synthesis puts A and B together into AB.

questions.q: The lecture describes synthesis as:
questions.e: Synthesis = construction; decomposition = demolition.

questions.q: Energy for a synthesis reaction usually comes in the form of:
questions.e: Requires energy input, usually heat.

questions.q: Forming functional proteins from amino acids is an example of:
questions.e: Building proteins = synthesis.

questions.q: The OPPOSITE of dehydration synthesis is:
questions.a: Hydrolysis (breaking a bond by adding water)
questions.e: Hydrolysis = break by adding water.

topics.10: Epidermis layers (Come Let's Get Sun Burned)
topics.16: Layers of the dermis and epidermis

questions.q: The cell cycle has two main stages. They are:
questions.e: Two stages: interphase, then mitosis (M phase).

questions.q: Which is the correct order of the cell cycle?
questions.e: Interphase (G1, S, G2) comes first, then mitosis.

questions.q: Interphase is made up of which three sub-phases?
questions.e: Interphase = G1, S, G2. Mitosis = PMAT.

questions.q: G1, S and G2 are all sub-phases of:
questions.e: Interphase has 3 sub-phases: G1, S, G2.

questions.q: Which part of the cell cycle is the longest?
questions.e: Interphase is the longest part; G1 is its first and longest phase.

questions.q: Is interphase a 'resting' phase?
questions.a: No — the cell is growing, working and preparing to divide
questions.e: Marieb says 'metabolic phase' would be a better name.

questions.q: Mitosis has how many sub-phases?
questions.e: Prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase (PMAT).

questions.q: What does 'G' stand for in G1 and G2?
questions.e: G1 = Gap/Growth phase 1; G2 = Gap/Growth phase 2.

questions.q: The cell cycle is defined as:
questions.a: The changes a cell goes through from when it forms until it divides
w: The making of proteins from mRNA
questions.e: Series of changes from formation to division.

questions.q: Which junction creates a leak-proof seal so nothing passes BETWEEN cells?
questions.e: Tight junctions fuse membranes like a zipper: an impermeable 'diffusion barrier'.

questions.q: Which junction lets neighboring cells COMMUNICATE by sharing ions and signals?
questions.e: Gap junctions = hollow connexon channels between two cells.

questions.q: Which junction acts like 'spot welds' to resist mechanical stress?
questions.e: Desmosomes = calcium-dependent interlocking proteins; 'spot welds'.

questions.q: Which junction anchors the BASAL surface of an epithelial cell to the basement membrane?
questions.e: Hemidesmosome = 'half' desmosome, connects cell to the CT below.

questions.q: The hollow protein channel that forms a gap junction is called a:
questions.e: Gap junction = hollow tube protein (connexon).

questions.q: Gap junctions are especially important in the heart because they:
questions.a: Let the electrical signal spread so the muscle contracts as a unit
w: Anchor the heart to the sternum
questions.e: Communication junction: heart, neurons, smooth muscle.

questions.q: Tight junctions in the blood-brain barrier and digestive tract act as a:
questions.e: Tight = impermeable seal.

questions.q: Where are tight junctions located on a cell?
questions.e: Tight = apical & lateral; desmosome = lateral; hemidesmosome = basal.

questions.q: In the skin, hemidesmosomes hold the:
questions.e: Hemidesmosome: between epidermis and dermis.

questions.q: Desmosomes are abundant in which two places?
questions.e: Places under high mechanical stress.

questions.q: Which is the ONLY dry membrane in the body?
questions.e: Cutaneous membrane = the skin.

questions.q: Which membrane lines body cavities CLOSED to the exterior?
questions.e: Serous = sealed (closed) cavities.

questions.q: Which membrane lines body cavities OPEN to the exterior?
questions.e: Mucosa: respiratory, digestive, urogenital tracts.

questions.q: Which membrane lines joint cavities, bursae and tendon sheaths?
questions.e: Synovial membrane makes synovial fluid.

questions.q: Which membrane has NO epithelial tissue?
questions.e: Synovial = loose areolar CT only; the connective tissue membrane.

questions.q: Serous membranes are made of:
questions.a: Simple squamous epithelium on areolar CT
w: Stratified squamous epithelium on dense CT
questions.e: Serosa: simple squamous on top of areolar CT.

questions.q: The layer of a serous membrane that touches the organ is the:
questions.e: Visceral = viscera (organ); parietal = body wall.

questions.q: The pleura, pericardium and peritoneum are all:
questions.e: Pleura (lungs), pericardium (heart), peritoneum (abdomen).

questions.q: The loose CT layer under a mucous membrane is called the:
questions.e: Mucosa = epithelium on loose CT (lamina propria).

questions.q: The cutaneous membrane is composed of:
w: Simple squamous epithelium and areolar CT
questions.e: Skin = epidermis + dermis.

questions.q: Which epithelium is found in the alveoli (air sacs) of the lungs and capillaries?
questions.e: One thin, flat layer: rapid diffusion and filtration.

questions.q: Which epithelium lines the kidney tubules and covers the ovaries?
questions.e: One layer of cube cells: secretion and absorption.

questions.q: Which epithelium lines the digestive tract from the stomach to the rectum?
questions.e: Tall cells with goblet cells: secretion and absorption.

questions.q: Which epithelium lines the urinary bladder?
questions.e: Transitional stretches to hold urine.

questions.q: The main function of simple squamous epithelium is:
questions.e: Thin = fast diffusion.

questions.q: Simple cuboidal epithelium looks like:
w: One layer of thin, flat cells
questions.e: Cuboidal = cube shaped; 'simple' = 1 layer.

questions.q: Which epithelium is associated with goblet cells and may have cilia, lining the uterus and fallopian tubes?
questions.e: Simple columnar: goblet cells, cilia specialization.

questions.q: In an epithelium's name, 'simple' means:
questions.e: First name = number of layers; last name = cell shape.

questions.q: 'Squamous' describes cells that are:
questions.e: Squamous = flat like fish scales.

questions.q: Which epithelium lines the ducts of some glands and functions in secretion and absorption?
questions.e: Simple cuboidal: kidney tubules, ovaries, gland ducts.

questions.q: In DNA, adenine (A) pairs with:
questions.e: DNA: A–T and G–C.

questions.q: In RNA, adenine (A) pairs with:
questions.e: RNA has no thymine; uracil replaces it.

questions.q: Guanine (G) always pairs with:
questions.e: G–C in both DNA and RNA.

questions.q: Which base is found in DNA but NOT in RNA?
questions.e: DNA: A, T, G, C. RNA: A, U, G, C.

questions.q: Which base is found in RNA but NOT in DNA?
questions.e: Uracil replaces thymine in RNA.

questions.q: Complementary bases are held together by:
questions.e: Weak hydrogen bonds, easily broken for replication.

questions.q: A nucleotide is made of:
questions.e: Three parts: phosphate, sugar, base.

questions.q: The 'rungs' of the DNA ladder are made of:
questions.e: Backbone = sugar-phosphate; rungs = bases.

questions.q: A memory trick for DNA pairing is that the straight letters pair and the curved letters pair. This means:
questions.e: Straight A & T; curved G & C.

questions.q: Which organelle packages and ships proteins, hormones, enzymes and lysosomes?
questions.e: Golgi = the cell's 'traffic director' / packaging center.

questions.q: Which organelle is the site of protein synthesis?
questions.e: Ribosomes make protein.

questions.q: Which organelle neutralizes toxins and alcohol?
questions.e: Peroxisome: oxidase enzymes detoxify; abundant in the liver.

questions.q: The Golgi body looks like:
questions.a: A stack of flattened membranous sacs near the nucleus
w: A bean-shaped organelle with folded cristae
Tiny red dots on the ER
questions.e: Stacked sacs near the nucleus.

questions.q: Peroxisomes are abundant in the liver because:
questions.a: The liver does much of the body's detoxification
w: The liver makes most of the body's protein
The liver needs the most ATP
questions.e: Peroxisomes neutralize toxins and alcohol.

questions.q: Ribosomes are produced by the:
questions.e: Nucleolus makes ribosomes; ribosomes make protein.

questions.q: Peroxisomes contain which type of enzyme?
questions.e: Peroxisomes = oxidase sacs; lysosomes = hydrolytic sacs.

questions.q: Ribosomes may be found:
questions.a: Free in the cytoplasm or attached to the ER
questions.e: Free ribosomes make proteins used inside the cell; ER-bound ones make proteins for export.

questions.q: Peroxisomes convert dangerous free radicals into:
questions.e: Free radicals → H₂O₂ → catalase turns it into water.

questions.q: Which is the TOP (most superficial) layer of the epidermis?
questions.e: Come (corneum) is first in 'Come Let's Get Sun Burned'.

questions.q: Which is the BOTTOM (deepest) layer of the epidermis?
questions.e: Burned (basale) is last; it sits on the basement membrane.

questions.q: From superficial to deep, the three layers are:
questions.e: Epidermis on top, dermis beneath, hypodermis below the skin.

questions.q: The superficial layer of the skin is the:
questions.e: Epidermis = superficial; dermis = deeper.

questions.q: Which dermal layer is on top, just under the epidermis?
questions.e: Papillary = superficial 1/5; reticular = deep 4/5.

questions.q: Which dermal layer is on the bottom?
questions.e: Reticular = the deep 4/5 of the dermis.

questions.q: The stratum basale sits directly on the:
questions.e: Deepest epidermal layer, on the basement membrane above the dermis.

questions.q: What lies BELOW the dermis?
questions.e: The hypodermis is not part of the skin; it sits below the dermis.

questions.q: All adult connective tissue develops from:
questions.e: Mesenchyme is the embryonic tissue all adult CT comes from.

questions.q: Mesenchyme is a type of:
questions.e: Embryonic CT: mesenchyme and Wharton's jelly.

questions.q: Where is mesenchyme found?
questions.e: Embryonic CT is only found in the embryo.

questions.q: The two types of embryonic connective tissue are:
questions.e: Embryonic CT: a) mesenchyme, b) Wharton's jelly.

questions.q: Wharton's jelly is found in the:
questions.e: Keeps the cord from kinking (patent = open).

questions.q: Bone, cartilage, blood and CT proper all come from:
questions.e: Remember: ALL adult CT develops from mesenchyme.

questions.q: Which statement about mesenchyme is TRUE?
questions.a: It is the embryonic tissue that gives rise to all adult connective tissue
w: It is the outer layer of the skin
It is found in the adult umbilical cord
It is a type of epithelium
questions.e: Mesenchyme = embryonic CT, source of all adult CT.

questions.q: Wharton's jelly keeps the umbilical cord 'patent,' which means:
questions.e: Patent = open.

questions.q: Which tissue is highly cellular with very little matrix?
questions.e: Epithelium: tightly packed cells, little matrix.

questions.q: Which tissue has LOTS of matrix and few cells?
questions.e: CT: not cellular, lots of matrix.

questions.q: Epithelium is avascular. This means it:
questions.a: Has little or no blood supply of its own
questions.e: Gets nutrients by diffusion from CT below.

questions.q: Which tissue is highly mitotic and replaces itself readily?
questions.e: Epithelium: highly mitotic. CT: not mitotic.

questions.q: Which tissue is generally very vascular (good blood supply)?
questions.e: CT is very vascular (cartilage is an exception).

questions.q: Epithelium has which two surfaces?
questions.e: Apical = free/exposed; basal = on the basement membrane.

questions.q: Connective tissue is described as almost the exact ___ of epithelial tissue.
questions.e: Epithelium: cellular, mitotic, avascular. CT: matrix, not mitotic, vascular.

questions.q: The main function of connective tissue is to:
questions.e: Epithelium covers; CT supports; muscle moves; nervous controls.

questions.q: The main function of epithelial tissue is to:
questions.e: Epithelium = covering.

questions.q: In 'Come Let's Get Sun Burned,' what does 'Let's' stand for?
questions.e: Corneum, Lucidum, Granulosum, Spinosum, Basale.

questions.q: In 'Come Let's Get Sun Burned,' what does 'Get' stand for?
questions.e: G = granulosum (the grainy layer).

questions.q: In 'Come Let's Get Sun Burned,' what does 'Sun' stand for?
questions.e: S = spinosum (the spiny layer).

questions.q: The correct order of the epidermis from superficial to deep is:
questions.e: Come Let's Get Sun Burned.

questions.q: Which layer lies directly beneath the stratum granulosum?
questions.e: ...Get (granulosum) Sun (spinosum) Burned (basale).

questions.q: Which layer is called the 'spiny layer' and contains Langerhans cells?
questions.e: Spines = pre-keratin bundles; Langerhans = phagocytic WBCs.

questions.q: Which layer is called the 'grainy layer'?
questions.e: Granules = pieces of dead organelles; cells filling with keratin.

questions.q: Melanocytes, which produce melanin, are found in the:
questions.e: Melanocytes are in the basale.

questions.q: Which layer lies directly above the stratum basale?
questions.e: Sun (spinosum) sits just above Burned (basale).

questions.q: Sudoriferous glands produce:
questions.e: Sudoriferous = sweat glands (eccrine and apocrine).

questions.q: Sebaceous glands produce:
questions.e: Sebaceous = oil glands; lubricate hair and skin.

questions.q: Ceruminous glands produce:
questions.e: Modified sweat glands in the ear canal.

questions.q: Which glands are attached to and empty into hair follicles and contain antibacterial lysozymes?
questions.e: Sebaceous: oil into the follicle; lysozymes kill bacteria.

questions.q: All cutaneous glands are what type of gland?
questions.e: Exocrine glands have ducts and live mostly in the dermis.

questions.q: Which sweat glands are small, very numerous, and open onto the skin through pores?
questions.e: Eccrine = temperature control.

questions.q: Which sweat glands are large, found in the axillary and urogenital regions, and become active at puberty?
questions.e: Apocrine: protein-rich sweat, opens into hair follicles.

questions.q: Ceruminous glands are a modified type of:
questions.e: Modified (apocrine) sweat glands in the external ear canal.

questions.q: Which is a function of earwax (cerumen)?
questions.a: Natural insect repellent and lubricates the ear canal
questions.e: Cerumen lubricates and repels insects.

questions.q: The main function of sudoriferous (sweat) glands is:
questions.e: Sweat evaporates to cool the body.

questions.q: Which epidermal layer is found ONLY in thick skin?
questions.e: Lucidum = the extra 5th layer.

questions.q: Where is thick skin found?
questions.a: Palms of the hands and soles of the feet
questions.e: Thick skin = palms & soles only.

questions.q: Thick skin has how many epidermal layers?
questions.e: Thick = 5 (adds lucidum); thin = 4.

questions.q: Thin skin has how many epidermal layers?
questions.e: Thin skin: corneum, granulosum, spinosum, basale.

questions.q: The stratum lucidum sits between which two layers?
questions.e: Come (corneum) Let's (lucidum) Get (granulosum).

questions.q: What does the stratum lucidum do?
questions.a: Adds protection and 'grip' so palms and soles don't slide
questions.e: Extra protection and grip for high-friction areas.

questions.q: A microscope slide shows a clear band between the corneum and granulosum. This skin is from:
questions.e: A visible lucidum means thick skin.

questions.q: 'Lucidum' means:
questions.e: Stratum lucidum = the 'clear layer'.

questions.q: Which receptor detects DEEP pressure? ('Think Pacific Ocean')
questions.e: Pacific Ocean is deep → Pacinian = deep pressure.

questions.q: Which receptor is responsible for two-point discrimination and light pressure?
questions.e: Meissner's: light touch, 2-point discrimination, in dermal papillae.

questions.q: Which receptor detects edges or points with light pressure?
questions.e: Merkel discs: edges/points, light pressure.

questions.q: Which receptor detects pain?
questions.e: Nociceptors = free nerve endings for painful stimuli.

questions.q: Per the lecture, which receptor detects HEAT? ('Sounds Italian; Italy is hot')
questions.e: Ruffini = hot (class pairing).

questions.q: Per the lecture, which receptor detects COLD? ('Sounds like Santa Claus')
questions.e: Krause = cold (class pairing).

questions.q: How many skin receptors were covered in lecture?
questions.e: Meissner, Merkel, Pacinian, nociceptor, Ruffini, Krause.

questions.q: Which receptor sits deepest in the skin?
questions.e: Deep dermis/hypodermis; light-touch receptors sit high.

questions.q: A light, feathery massage stroke mainly stimulates:
questions.e: Light touch receptors sit near the epidermis.

questions.q: Meissner's corpuscles are housed in the:
questions.e: Papillae house touch receptors.

questions.q: Transitional epithelium is found in the:
questions.e: Urinary system: bladder, ureters.

questions.q: What makes transitional epithelium unique?
questions.a: It is the only epithelium capable of stretching
w: It is only one cell thick
It is found only in the skin
questions.e: Cells change shape as the bladder fills.

questions.q: When transitional epithelium is NOT stretched, the apical cells are:
questions.e: Relaxed = dome (umbrella) cells.

questions.q: When the bladder is full and transitional epithelium is stretched, the apical cells become:
questions.e: Stretched = flat surface cells.

questions.q: The function of transitional epithelium is:
questions.a: Protection and stretching to hold fluid
questions.e: Lets the bladder hold urine.

questions.q: Transitional epithelium has how many layers?
questions.e: It is a stratified (multi-layer) epithelium.

questions.q: The dome-shaped apical cells of transitional epithelium are sometimes called:
questions.e: Umbrella-shaped cells at the apical surface.

questions.q: Why is the bladder lined with transitional epithelium?
questions.a: So it can fill with urine without tearing
questions.e: Stretches like a rubber band.

questions.q: Which is thicker, the epidermis or the dermis?
w: Neither; the stratum corneum is thickest
questions.e: The dermis is much thicker than the epidermis.

questions.q: The thickest layer of the EPIDERMIS is the:
questions.e: About 30–40 cells thick, ~3/4 of the epidermis.

questions.q: The stratum corneum makes up about how much of the epidermis?
questions.e: Corneum ≈ 3/4 of epidermal thickness.

questions.q: Which dermal layer is the larger (thicker) one?
questions.e: Reticular = 4/5; papillary = 1/5.

questions.q: Which dermal layer is the smaller (thinner) one?
questions.e: Papillary = superficial 1/5.

questions.q: Which epidermal layers are described as only 'a few cells thick'?
questions.e: Lucidum: a few cells thick. Granulosum: only a few cells thick.

questions.q: How many cells thick is the stratum corneum (per the slides)?
questions.e: Slide: 30–40 cells (Marieb says 20–30 rows).

questions.q: What is the largest organ of the body?
questions.e: The skin (cutaneous membrane) is the largest organ.

questions.q: The dermis has two layers. They are:
questions.e: Dermis: papillary (superficial), reticular (deep).

questions.q: The papillary layer of the dermis is made of:
questions.e: Papillary = areolar (loose) CT.

questions.q: The reticular layer of the dermis is made of:
questions.e: Reticular = dense irregular CT, strong in all directions.

questions.q: Hair follicles, sweat glands, oil glands and lamellar corpuscles are found in which layer?
questions.e: Reticular layer contains epidermal derivatives.

questions.q: The epidermis is made mostly of:
questions.e: Epidermis = KSS; avascular.

questions.q: Which is vascular (has blood vessels)?
questions.e: Epidermis is avascular; dermis is vascular.

questions.q: Dermal papillae project from the dermis into the:
questions.e: Papillae push up into the epidermis.

questions.q: Thin skin, superficial to deep, is:
questions.e: Thin skin has no lucidum.

questions.q: Which statement about the hypodermis is TRUE?
questions.a: It is NOT a layer of skin; it is subcutaneous fat
w: It is the deepest layer of the epidermis
It is part of the dermis
questions.e: Hypodermis = subcutaneous layer below the dermis.

questions.q: The four phases of mitosis, in order, are:
questions.e: PMAT.

questions.q: In which phase do chromosomes line up in the middle of the cell?
questions.e: 'Meet in the Middle in Metaphase.'

questions.q: In which phase are chromosomes pulled to opposite ends of the cell?
questions.e: 'Away in Anaphase.'

questions.q: In which phase does the nuclear membrane fall apart and chromatin condense into chromosomes?
questions.e: Prophase: membrane & nucleolus break down, spindle forms, centrioles move apart.

questions.q: In which phase does the nuclear membrane reform and cytokinesis occur?
questions.e: Telophase is like prophase in reverse.

questions.q: Which is the LONGEST phase of mitosis?
questions.e: Prophase = 1st and longest phase of mitosis.

questions.q: Cytokinesis is the:
questions.a: Division of the cytoplasm that splits the cell in two
questions.e: Cyto = cell; kinesis = motion.

questions.q: The pinch in the middle of a dividing cell during telophase is the:
questions.e: Cleavage furrow pinches the cell in two.

questions.q: Mitosis turns one mother cell into:
w: Two cells with half the DNA each
questions.e: 1 mother cell → 2 daughter cells with the same genes.

questions.q: During prophase, the centrioles:
questions.a: Move to opposite ends of the cell
questions.e: Each pair of centrioles moves to opposite poles and forms the spindle.

questions.q: Which organelle is called the 'suicide sac' of the cell?
questions.e: If lysosomes rupture, the cell digests itself.

questions.q: Lysosomes contain which type of enzymes?
questions.e: Lysosomes = digestive enzyme sacs; peroxisomes = oxidase sacs.

questions.q: Which organelle breaks down bacteria, viruses, dirt and worn-out cell parts?
questions.e: Lysosomes 'break things down'.

questions.q: Lysosomes are packaged by the:
questions.e: The Golgi packages enzymes, hormones and lysosomes.

questions.q: Peroxisomes are similar to lysosomes, but they:
questions.a: Neutralize toxins and alcohol with oxidase enzymes
questions.e: Peroxisome = detox; lysosome = digestion.

questions.q: Which organelle has NO membrane and makes protein?
questions.e: Ribosomes are tiny protein + rRNA bodies; site of protein synthesis.

questions.q: What keeps a lysosome's enzymes from destroying the cell?
questions.e: Membrane keeps the hydrolytic enzymes contained.

questions.q: Lysosomes are especially abundant in:
questions.a: Phagocytes (white blood cells that eat bacteria)
questions.e: Phagocytes rely on lysosomes to digest what they engulf.

questions.q: Match: 'packages' → ?, 'makes protein' → ?, 'detoxifies' → ?, 'digests' → ?
questions.e: Golgi packages; ribosome makes protein; peroxisome detoxifies; lysosome digests.

questions.q: Which fiber is the STRONGEST, with very high tensile strength?
questions.e: Collagen resists pulling, compression and deformity.

questions.q: Which fiber can stretch and RECOIL to its original shape?
questions.e: Elastic = stretch and recoil like a rubber band.

questions.q: Which fibers are skinny, highly branched collagen fibers that form a support network for soft organs?
questions.e: Reticular: internal 'skeleton' of spleen, lymph nodes.

questions.q: Which cells make and secrete the fibers into the matrix?
questions.e: Fibroblasts secrete fibers into the ground substance.

questions.q: The intercellular matrix has two components:
questions.e: Matrix = ground substance + fibers.

questions.q: Reticular fibers compared to regular collagen fibers are:
questions.e: 'Skinny collagen fibers'; not as strong.

questions.q: Elastic connective tissue (rich in elastic fibers) is found in the:
questions.a: Vocal cords, lungs and large blood vessels
questions.e: Structures that must stretch and spring back.

questions.q: Tendons and ligaments are made primarily of which fiber?
questions.e: Dense regular CT: parallel collagen bundles.

questions.q: Which tissue contains all three fiber types and is the body's 'packing material'?
questions.e: Areolar has collagen, elastic and reticular fibers.

questions.q: The three fiber types are:
questions.e: Collagen, reticular, elastic.

questions.q: In which epidermal layer are ALL of the cells dead?
questions.e: Corneum: all cells dead, keratinized.

questions.q: In which layer do some cells start to die as they fill with keratin and move away from the blood supply?
questions.e: Granulosum: some alive, some beginning to die.

questions.q: Why do epidermal cells die as they move upward?
questions.a: They get farther from the blood supply in the dermis
w: They are attacked by Langerhans cells
questions.e: The epidermis is avascular; nutrients diffuse up from the dermis.

questions.q: Which layer is made of living cells actively dividing?
questions.e: Basale: mitosis, nearest the blood supply.

questions.q: Which of these layers is made of DEAD cells?
questions.e: Lucidum = a few rows of flat, dead cells.

questions.q: Which two layers contain living cells?
questions.e: Deep layers near the blood supply are alive.

questions.q: Dead cells of the stratum corneum are filled with which protein?
questions.e: Keratin makes the corneum tough and waterproof.

questions.q: Going from deep to superficial, epidermal cells go from:
questions.a: Alive and dividing to dead and keratinized
questions.e: Born in the basale, shed from the corneum.

questions.q: In which phase does DNA replication occur?
questions.e: S = Synthesis; DNA is doubled.

questions.q: In which phase does the cell grow to its mature size?
questions.e: G1 = Growth 1, the first and longest phase.

questions.q: In which phase does the cell do 'housekeeping' and final preparation before mitosis?
questions.e: G2 = final preparation.

questions.q: What happens in the M phase?
w: The cell grows to mature size
questions.e: M = mitosis (cell division).

questions.q: At the end of G1, which structures replicate?
questions.e: Centrioles replicate at the end of G1.

questions.q: A cell that never divides (does not do mitosis) stays in which phase?
questions.e: Some cells never leave G1.

questions.q: What does 'S' stand for in the S phase?
questions.e: S = synthesis of DNA.

questions.q: A cell enters S phase with 46 chromosomes. When it leaves S phase it has:
questions.e: DNA is doubled into sister chromatids.

questions.q: Why must DNA replication happen BEFORE mitosis?
questions.a: So each daughter cell gets a full set of 46 chromosomes
questions.e: Each daughter cell needs the right number of chromosomes (23 pairs).

questions.q: Which layer of the epidermis makes new cells?
questions.e: The epidermis grows from the basale.

questions.q: The stratum basale is also known as the:
questions.e: Germinativum = germinating, where new cells form.

questions.q: Cells in the stratum basale are undergoing:
questions.e: Constantly dividing by mitosis.

questions.q: The epidermis grows in which direction?
questions.e: New cells form in the basale and are pushed toward the surface.

questions.q: Cells of the stratum basale are what shape?
questions.e: Cells are cuboidal (to columnar).

questions.q: Why is the germinating layer the deepest layer of the epidermis?
questions.a: It is closest to the blood supply in the dermis
w: It is farthest from the blood supply
questions.e: Dividing cells need nutrients diffusing from the dermis.

questions.q: Which pair is located in the germinating layer?
questions.e: Basale: mitosis + melanocytes.

questions.q: Cutaneous glands form from cells of which layer that push down into the dermis?
questions.e: Glands come from basale cells growing down.

questions.q: Which layer is responsible for fingerprints?
questions.e: Dermal papillae form the fingerprint ridges.

questions.q: Fingerprints are formed by:
questions.e: Projections of the dermis into the epidermis.

questions.q: Besides forming fingerprints, dermal papillae:
questions.a: Bring capillaries close to the epidermis and house touch receptors
questions.e: Papillae: fingerprints, grip, capillaries, touch receptors.

questions.q: The fingerprint ridges help with:
questions.e: Ridges create friction for grip.

questions.q: The papillary layer, which forms fingerprints, makes up how much of the dermis?
questions.e: Papillary = superficial 1/5.

questions.q: The papillary layer that forms fingerprints is made of which tissue?
questions.e: Papillary layer = areolar CT.

questions.q: Fingerprints are part of which main skin region?
questions.e: They come from the papillary layer of the dermis.

questions.q: Footprints on the soles are formed the same way as fingerprints, by the:
questions.e: Papillae form ridge patterns on palms and soles.

questions.q: What do goblet cells produce?
questions.e: Goblet cells make mucus.

questions.q: Goblet cells are associated with which two epithelia?
questions.e: Both columnar epithelia have goblet cells.

questions.q: Goblet cells are named for their:
questions.e: The cup-shaped cell that secretes mucus.

questions.q: In the respiratory tract, mucus from goblet cells acts as a:
questions.a: Sticky trap for dust, swept away by cilia
questions.e: Pseudostratified ciliated epithelium: goblet cells + cilia.

questions.q: Where would you expect to find goblet cells?
questions.e: Simple columnar epithelium of the digestive tract.

questions.q: Goblet cells are found in which type of tissue?
questions.e: They sit within columnar epithelium.

questions.q: The upper respiratory tract is lined with pseudostratified columnar epithelium with cilia and:
questions.e: Goblet cells make the mucus the cilia sweep.

questions.q: Which statement about goblet cells is TRUE?
w: They anchor cells to the basement membrane
questions.e: Goblet = mucus.

questions.q: The watery (liquid) portion of the cytoplasm is the:
questions.e: Cytosol = watery portion; in the Jello analogy it is the Jello.

questions.q: Which structure is the 'brain' of the cell and contains DNA?
questions.e: The nucleus directs all cellular functions.

questions.q: Which organelle is a 'tubular transport system' connected to the nuclear envelope?
questions.e: ER = membrane canals for intracellular transport.

questions.q: Rough ER is 'rough' because it is:
questions.e: Rough ER makes proteins; smooth ER has no ribosomes.

questions.q: Smooth ER is responsible for:
questions.a: Lipid and carbohydrate synthesis and breaking down drugs
questions.e: No ribosomes, so no protein; lipids and detox.

questions.q: A cell with 2 nuclei is described as:
questions.e: Binucleate ≠ multinucleate (3+).

questions.q: A mature red blood cell has no nucleus. It is:
questions.e: Anucleate = no nucleus.

questions.q: In the 'Jello fruit salad' analogy for cytoplasm, the fruit represents the:
questions.e: Jello = cytosol; fruit = organelles.

questions.q: The nucleus is surrounded by the:
questions.e: Double phospholipid bilayer with nuclear pores.

questions.q: Ribosomes are:
questions.e: Ribosomes make protein, free or on the rough ER.
